title: Integer literals
note: Draft maps bigint to Integer, but JavaScript number to Number. Rust i64 is bounded. Python int and JavaScript bigint have different numeric models. These examples all represent 2.

title: Name a value
note: HashQL let binds within its body. Draft supplies that body from the rest of the callback. Python names can be rebound, and JavaScript const does not make an object's contents immutable. HashQL values are immutable.

title: Compare values
note: HashQL conditions require Boolean, not a truthy value. These primitive comparisons produce true in every column. Equality for richer values differs between the host languages. These examples compare integers only.

title: Choose a value
note: All examples choose 2. Draft runs both branch callbacks during construction. HashQL evaluates only the selected branch. A Draft callback is not a HashQL closure. Without else, HashQL if returns Option instead.

codes.rust:
let foo = 2_i64;
let value = if foo == 2 { foo } else { 0 };
codes.python:
foo = 2
value = foo if foo == 2 else 0
codes.typescript:
const foo = 2n;
const value = foo === 2n ? foo : 0n;
codes.reference:
let foo = 2 in
if foo == 2 then foo else 0

title: Build a struct and read a field
note: The result is 2. HashQL structs are structural and immutable. Rust uses a named struct, Python uses a dictionary, and TypeScript uses an object. HashQL rejects missing fields at compile time. Python dictionary lookup can raise KeyError. Current Draft let requires an expression handle for this struct, not a plain object.

codes.typescript:
const person = { value: 2n, label: "two" };
const value = person.value;

title: Read a fixed tuple position
note: The result is 2. HashQL access uses a fixed zero-based position checked at compile time. Draft [0] constructs that access, not list indexing. Python checks bounds at runtime. TypeScript's tuple annotation does not freeze its array. The illustrative functional cell borrows the reference notation's tuple-literal spelling.

codes.typescript:
const foo: readonly [bigint, string] = [2n, "two"];
const value = foo[0];

title: Look up a list element
note: At position 0, Rust returns Some(2), Python returns 2, and TypeScript returns 2n. HashQL index is specified to return Some(2), or None() when missing. The current SDK $index instead describes Integer | Null. That descriptor mismatch is unresolved: serialization below does not prove runtime null behavior. Rust get is checked. Python [] raises IndexError out of range (and accepts negative positions). JavaScript [] returns undefined when missing.

codes.reference:
let foo = [2, 3] in
let position = 0 in
foo[position]

title: Capture a binding in a function
note: The call returns true. General HashQL closure construction is not supported by Draft yet (BE-1015), so its cell is unavailable. A Draft.program or if callback is not a HashQL closure. Python closures capture a binding that could later be rebound. This example never rebinds foo.

codes.python:
foo = 2
def matches_foo(value: int) -> bool:
    return value == foo
value = matches_foo(2)
codes.functional:
(let foo 2
  (let matches_foo
    (fn [] {value: Integer} Boolean
      (eq value foo))
    (matches_foo 2)))
codes.reference:
let foo = 2,
    matches_foo = (value: Integer): Boolean -> value == foo
in
matches_foo(2)

title: Import under another name
note: Each call returns true. Rust uses the cmp fixture in the common setup. Python uses operator.eq. TypeScript uses Node's isDeepStrictEqual. They are host imports with different general equality semantics. Draft import instead adds a scoped HashQL use declaration. It does not load a host module.

codes.python:
from operator import eq as same
foo = 2
value = same(foo, 2)
codes.reference:
use(::core::cmp, {eq: same},
  let foo = 2 in
  same(foo, 2))

title: State a compatible type
note: Draft has no builder for HashQL as. Typed let is not that operation. HashQL verifies that the inferred type is a subtype of the asserted type, leaving the value unchanged. The host examples use checked annotations, not unchecked TypeScript assertions. Rust has no corresponding Integer <: Number relationship and uses a floating-point literal instead. Python annotations are not runtime checks.

codes.rust:
let foo: f64 = 2.0;
let value = foo;
codes.typescript:
const foo: number = 2;
const value = foo;
codes.reference:
let foo = 2 as Number in
foo

title: Give a type another name
note: Count is an alias, not a distinct type or a non-negative constraint. Python uses the TypeAlias spelling supported before Python 3.12 too. Draft's third let argument annotates the binding. The functional/reference cells use as to constrain its initializer instead. These are analogous programs, not claims of identical emitted syntax. The HashQL compiler checks annotations. Draft construction does not validate the annotation against its initializer.

codes.python:
from typing import TypeAlias
Count: TypeAlias = int
foo: Count = 2
value = foo
codes.reference:
type Count = Integer in
let foo = 2 as Count in
foo

title: Introduce a distinct type
note: HashQL newtype and the Rust tuple struct create distinct types. Python NewType distinguishes types for static checkers but returns the original int at runtime: it is not a wrapper. The TypeScript class is a runtime wrapper. Its private payload makes its instance type distinct from an otherwise identical class. None of these declarations adds a range check.

codes.python:
from typing import NewType
Count = NewType("Count", int)
foo = Count(2)
value = foo
codes.reference:
newtype Count = Integer in
let foo = Count(2) in
foo
